content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to automatically build a dictionary (or more precisely, a concordance) by clustering context-dependent BERT word embeddings. The technique is applied to SemEval test sets in order to compare with reference word senses, and also to the works of Shakespeare.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

The task of automatic dictionary construction is interesting and potentially very useful in low-resource settings.

Weakness:

This seems to be exploratory work. The paper uses a basic off-the-shelf model and clustering algorithm, and tests it out on SemEval corpora using a general clustering-distance metric. In most cases, the algorithm doesn’t significantly outperform assigning just one sense per word, but the authors don’t delve into why this might be. They move on to generating a similar clustering for words in the works of Shakespeare, and provide a qualitative analysis that highlights some non-intuitive groupings.

Missing highly-relevant publication:

Xingwei He and Siu Ming Yiu. 2022. Controllable Dictionary Example Generation: Generating Example Sentences for Specific Targeted Audiences. In Proceedings of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), pages 610–627, Dublin, Ireland. Association for Computational Linguistics.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper aims to "help" people to build dictionaries by using corpora and by using BERT. The motivation is taken from the colossal use of work in building the Deutsches Worterbuch. According to what is described in the paper, the challenge of building such a dictionary was similar to the challenge of building a cathedral.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
PROS
- the paper proposes the task of automatic dictionary generation (ADG)
- the paper proposes a methodology to evaluate ADG 


CONS
- ADG is not at all novel task
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The major problem of the paper is the lack of novelty or, at least, the lack of explanation why the method proposed in this paper innovate with respect to existing methods or proposals.
Indeed, there is a large bunch of papers and a semeval 2022 competition that has been overlooked:
Task 1: CODWOE - COmparing Dictionaries and WOrd Embeddings 
The introduction to this competition brings many papers that should be at least referred to.
Moreover, there are also ACL papers that appeared in 2022 with related topics, e.g.:
Ruzzetti et al., Lacking the Embedding of a Word? Look it up into a Traditional Dictionary
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper fails to convince about its innovativeness and, therefore, it is hard to judge.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addressed the task of generating a set of senses from a corpus. Specifically, the authors studied a method for grouping contextual embeddings into clusters of word senses and left the gloss generation task for future work. In the experiments, the authors investigated the agglomerative hierarchical clustering method to cluster contextual embeddings produced by CharacterBERT. An initial experiment with WSD corpora revealed that the method had a slightly better performance as measured by ARI than a simple baseline where all occurrences of the same "token" are clustered together. Additional experiments on the Shakespeare corpus (unlabeled) showed some interesting qualitative results. Finally, the authors discussed challenges including the lack of a proper evaluation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper proposed an interesting task.

Weaknesses:
1. Clustering contextual embeddings have been studied extensively in many different contexts and purposes. Several methods could inform or improve the methods (AHC) used in the paper. For example
    - [Is Neural Topic Modelling Better than Clustering? An Empirical Study on Clustering with Contextual Embeddings for Topics](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.09874.pdf)
    - [TUE at SemEval-2020 Task 1: Detecting semantic change by clustering contextual word embeddings](https://aclanthology.org/2020.semeval-1.28.pdf)
    - [Isotropy in the Contextual Embedding Space: Clusters and Manifolds ](https://openreview.net/forum?id=xYGNO86OWDH)
2. With the lack of a strong evaluation, it is really hard to propose a task that yields a productive discussion on the matter.
3. Glosses are an important part of a dictionary (in a human sense) and they allowed additional evaluation methods as well. There are related works that "learn" to generate gloss without changing the embeddings:
    - [Definition modeling: learning to define word embeddings in natural language](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/3298023.3298042)
    - [Conditional Generators of Words Definitions](http://arxiv.org/abs/1806.10090)
4. The method achieved a significantly higher ARI than the baseline in SemEval2007, but it was unclear why this was the case.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear with a few explanations omitted such as a discussion on SemEval2007 or why ADG is more interesting in a not-able-to-evaluate corpus like Shakespeare. In terms of quality, the proposed task came with an automated evaluation based on WSD, but the experiments did not investigate the challenges (such as sense number distribution or generalized toward other corpora). In addition, the qualitative evaluation could be more thoroughly such as an investigation to explain why the method generated more senses than words.
content.summary_of_the_review: Even though the paper presented an interesting case of contextual word embedding, it did not make itself clear why the task of clustering vectors was novel and meaningful to the dictionary generation. In addition, the experiments did not reveal strong results in both quantitative and qualitative. Thus, I do not recommend this paper to ICLR.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposed a BERT based method (Grimm's BERT) to generate dictionaries automatically from unlabeled corpus, just like what Grimm brothers did in the past. The algorithm has two parts: 1) turn word tokens into contextual embedding vectors with CharacterBERT, 2) cluster all the tokens into senses based on semantic distance with hierarchical clustering. Quantitative evaluation was done with public semeval/semcor datasets, with no clustering and single cluster as baseline and Adjusted Rand Index as the metric. The results showed that Grimm's BERT is significantly better on semeval 2007 data but not others. The paper also applied the method to Shakespear's work and gave some examples on what worked what not. The paper concludes that the method "does not give perfect results yet" and could be a tool for linguists.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

1) Good story. The task of recreating Grimm's dictionary with modern tools is interesting.

Weakness

1) The paper didn't address most of the key parts in Grimm's task: how to decide which token is dictionary-worthy? how to generate gloss? how to deal with inaccuracies in the clustering, which is inevitable? The paper started a grand task but only covered some very basic aspects of it with off-the-shelf tools.

2) Evaluation. For clustering, the baseline is too weak (no cluster and one cluster). For the end-to-end ADG task, there's no quantitative evaluation at all.

3) ADG itself is an old topic in NLP (I would not try to pull out historical papers). Claiming to do it the first is not convincing, esp when the methodology and evaluation are weak.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: ok. The Reviewer had no trouble following the paper's content.

Quality: weak. The evaluation is weak with trivial baseline and no quantitative evaluation on the end-to-end results.

Novelty: weak. This is a classical NLP task, and the paper used off-the-shelf tools.

Reproducibility: ok. The models and dataset used are mostly off-the-shelf, The authors promised to share experiment code/data after the review.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The Reviewer recommends rejection.

Reason towards rejection: old topic; weak, off-the-shelf method; didn't cover the key aspects (token selection, clustering result post processing, gloss etc) for a real Grimm-replica task; evaluation is weak without good baseline and quantitative numbers for end-to-end task.

Reason towards acceptance: if the paper showed a true end-to-end reproduction of publication-ready level dictionary, even just for English, without significant human intervention, that would have been some achievement. However that's not the case.

content.title: Automatic Dictionary Generation: Could Brothers Grimm Create a Dictionary with BERT?
content.abstract: The creation of the most famous German dictionary, also referred to as ``Deutsches Wörterbuch'' or in English ``The German Dictionary'', by the two brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, took more than a lifetime to be finished (1838--1961). In our work we examine the question, if it would be possible for them to create a dictionary using present technology, i.e., language models such as BERT. Starting with the definition of the task of Automatic Dictionary Generation, we propose a method based on contextualized word embeddings and hierarchical clustering to create a dictionary given unannotated text corpora.  We justify our design choices by running variants of our method on English texts, where ground truth dictionaries are available.  Finally, we apply of our approach to Shakespeare's work and automatically generate a dictionary tailored to Shakespearean vocabulary and contexts without human intervention.
